p: At Sterling her father finally said it. He hit Travis Hensley first, in the bar, because the man had his hands on a kid. Then he called the kid nobody.
He still says he went home alone, and he said yes to giving the lab his DNA.
Dani took his bishop at last, with the pawn that didn't open her king to his queen.
Ronnie remembered that every time her father came up he ordered a beer and a Sprite, and later on just the Sprite. He'd figured one of the crew was driving.
On the back of the envelope Dani wrote a new question. Who was the kid?
Luis Ruiz. At Sterling. May's his birthday month.
Ana Brennan. Waiting on the district attorney's answer to the motion.
Gene Vigil. The retired detective who gave Dani his notebook.
Meredith Sloane. The chief deputy district attorney on the other side of the motion.

Wednesday, May 5, at seven, she sat on her step with the phone in her lap and the basement light on, and the phone didn't ring. At ten after she checked that it was charged. At half past she went up to the kitchen and stood there with the phone in her hand. In all the years of Wednesdays he'd missed four, and every one of those had been a lockdown she only heard about from him, a week late.

Thursday, May 6, at seven, it rang. The recording, and then him. It's Thursday, he said. I know what day it is, Pa. Sixty two. I traded Oscar my Wednesday for his Thursday. I wanted to hear you on the day.

Her card had come. He read her the inside of it like she hadn't written it, slow, with his reading glasses on, she could tell. Somebody on the tier had made a cake out of crushed cookies and peanut butter in a commissary bag and stuck a match in it. Rudy sang. Rudy can't sing, he said. Nobody told him in time.

Since Sterling it had sat on the kitchen table exactly the way she'd left it, her pawn on the square where his bishop used to be, his queen at the far end of the file that hadn't opened. Both Wednesdays since, he'd said the same thing. He said it again. I'm still looking at it.
I told Teo what you said. About the pawn. A long breath on the line. What'd he say? Nothing. That's him saying something, her father said.

Meredith Sloane's answer to the motion had come in on Monday. She'd asked the court for two more weeks and gotten them and used every day. Ana had read it on her phone at a red light, she said, and sat through the green. Tuesday, she'd said. Bring a calculator. Meredith brought numbers.

Saturday, May 8, she took her first whole PrepTest on LawHub, the official kind, retired questions from the people who write the test, on the same screens she'd see in June. A study room at the library from eight to noon, door shut, her phone out in the car so she couldn't touch it at the break. Ten minutes after the second section by the clock on the wall, and not a minute more. She treated every section as if it counted, because in June she wouldn't know which one didn't.

It came back lower than she wanted. She'd known it would, and it still sat in her stomach the whole way home. Twenty three wrong, and nine of those in the last section, where she'd started to hurry. Four of the misses had numbers in them.
She sent Ana the count from the driveway. Ana wrote back in under a minute, which for Ana was a phone call.
A text from Ana. Good. Now we know where you are. Don't look at the answers yet. Redo every one you flagged or weren't sure of, no clock, and write one line on each saying why. Then look.

Sunday was Mother's Day. She did the twenty three at the kitchen table under Ma's lanyard, no clock, the way Ma did her charting, one line each. She fixed eleven of her misses before she ever opened the key. The other twelve she got wrong a second time, most of them the same way. Ana said those were two different problems. The eleven were the clock. The twelve were the study plan.
May on Federal. The laundromat has its door propped open for the first time this year, the draft comes up the stairs smelling like dryer sheets, and Dicta has moved her whole self into it. Pencil.

This test has no math on it. It has numbers anyway, in a few questions on every test, and nearly all of them break the same way. Somebody moves from a share to a count, or from a count to a share, and hopes you don't notice the move.

A share is a part of something. Nine percent of the accidents. One in five people in the room. A count is how many. Twenty one men. Four burglaries. They answer different questions, and an argument that needs one of them can't run on the other. Complaints about the bus line were a smaller share of the city's complaints this year? Fine. If the city got twice as many complaints, a smaller share can still be more complaints about the bus. Burglaries on your street doubled? Doubled from two is four.

Averages hide things too. An average is a total divided by a count, and one huge number in the total can drag it anywhere. One neighbor's lottery win can raise the average income on a street where nobody else got a raise. When an argument moves from an average to what's ordinary or typical, ask what went into the total.

So when you see a percent, ask of what, and how many. When you see a raw number, ask out of how many. When you see an average, ask what's in it. The trap answers will be very confident about whichever one the argument handed you.

How the exam asks it. Watch for flaw and weaken questions built on percentages, rates or totals. The right answer usually names the missing number: the total, the size of the group, or what the percent was taken of.

Then there's where the numbers came from. A sample is a small group standing in for a big one, and it's only as good as the way it got picked. People who fill out a comment card. People who answer a poll on a website. The fights somebody phoned in to the police. Each of those groups picked itself, and a group that picks itself tends to share whatever you're trying to measure.

Size matters less than people think. Four hundred people chosen at random can tell you a lot. Four hundred people who chose to answer can tell you about people who choose to answer. When an answer says the sample was too small, check whether it's the size that's wrong or the picking. On this test it's usually the picking.

Police files are samples too, by the way, and nobody ever calls them that. A detective's experience is the cases somebody reported to him. The fights that ended quietly out back, with nobody watching, never made it into his notebook, so they never made it into his rule.
How the exam asks it. Stems ask what the argument overlooks, or takes for granted, about its survey or study. Ask how the people in it got there before you ask how many there were.

Most kitchen fires start while somebody's home. My sister read that in a magazine once and wanted to cook with the front door open, I never found out why. Nearly all cooking happens while somebody's home. A number about when most of the fires start tells you nothing until you set it next to when most of the cooking happens. That comparison number is the base rate: how common a thing is in the whole population before you know anything else.

It cuts the other way as well. A base rate tells you what a trait alone is worth. Twenty red jackets in a room, and the jacket alone points at any one of the twenty. But a base rate treats every one of the twenty as the same, and they rarely are. Add one fact that sets a person apart and the base rate stops being the whole story. An argument that leans on a base rate gets weaker with anything that makes the group's members unequal.

How the exam asks it. Stems ask which fact most weakens an argument from frequencies, or what it fails to consider. The answer is often the comparison number nobody gave you, or a fact that makes one member of the group different from the rest.

An evaluate question asks what you'd most want to know to judge an argument. The answers are questions, or whether clauses, and the right one has an odd property. Answer it yes and the argument gets stronger. Answer it no and it gets weaker. Either way it moves.

So test each choice twice. Imagine the answer is yes. Then imagine no. If one of them leaves the argument exactly where it was, that choice is gone. The usual wrong answer helps a lot if it comes back one way and does nothing the other way. The next most usual is a question that's interesting and has nothing to do with the conclusion.

Try it on a small one. A woman says her tomatoes did better this year because she switched fertilizers. Would you want to know whether her neighbor's tomatoes, on the old fertilizer, also did better this year? Yes. If they did, it was probably the weather. If they didn't, the fertilizer looks good. It moves both ways, so it's the one.

Call it the two answer test, and do some of the work before you read the choices. Find the gap, then ask which single fact would close it or open it wider. That fact, put as a question, is usually the answer. Work one. A ski hill says its new helmets have made the slopes safer, because nobody had a head injury this season and three people did last season. What would be most useful to know to evaluate the argument? Whether as many skiers fell this season. If they did, the helmets were tested and held, and the argument gets stronger. If hardly anybody fell, the helmets never had a chance to do anything, and the argument has nothing under it. That one variable, how often the helmets were needed, decides it.

Two wrong answers you'll see again and again. Whether the new helmets cost more is interesting and touches nothing in the conclusion. Whether the old helmets were ever recalled helps a little if the answer is yes and does nothing if it's no, so it fails the test. Variation: some stems ask for the answer to which question would most help, and some give you whether clauses. Same test either way. When two choices both pass, take the one that goes at the conclusion's exact claim. Safer is the claim here. Not cheaper, not more popular.
How the exam asks it. Stems ask which would be most useful to know, or which question's answer would most help in evaluating the argument. Run every choice as a yes and then as a no.

Records are the dullest papers in a case file and some of the most useful. A property log, a lab sheet, a dispatch line. When a passage is a record, read it three ways. What does it state? Dates, places, what was done, in its own words. What does it let you infer? The thing nobody wrote down but somebody must have done or believed. And whose voice is in it? A clerk who types up what a detective said hasn't said they agree.

That last one matters on attitude questions. A dry document usually has a dry author, and neutral can be the right answer when a passage only reports. It's rarer on full passages, where most authors lean one way, and indifferent is almost never right. But look for the one line where somebody's reasoning got written down, and keep it attached to the person it came from.

And read the dates. A clerk writes received, stored, returned and audited in that order because that's the order things happened to the bag. Nobody wrote it to win anything, which is why it can be worth more than most of the arguments in the file.

How the exam asks it. Stems ask what the passage states, what can be inferred from it, the author's attitude, or which fact would most weaken a claim in it. Keep a quoted view with the person quoted. A record usually keeps time better than the people in it did, so check the dates before you trust anybody's memory of them.
Saturday you took a real one, start to finish, and the number was lower than you wanted. It's supposed to be, the first time. What you do on Sunday counts for more than what you did on Saturday.

Before you look at a single answer, go back through every question you flagged or weren't sure of. No clock. Answer it again, and write one line for each: why this choice and not the other four. That's called blind review, and it sorts your misses in two. Some you get right once you have time. Those are pacing, and you fix them with timed sections. Some you still get wrong. Those are skill, and you fix them by going back to the chapter that teaches them.

Then open the key and keep a log, one line a miss. The question type. The trap you took: too strong, the reversed arrow, true but beside the point. And the words in the passage that should have stopped you. After three tests the log will tell you what to study better than I can.

Take the official PrepTests on LawHub, timed, the way you did Saturday, and review every one before you take the next. Our questions teach the skill. Theirs are the real thing, and they tell you where you are.
It's the same as reading a record. You don't read the verdict and then go looking for the transcript that fits it. You read cold, decide, and then you check.

How the exam asks it. LawHub has official PrepTests in the real test interface. Take them under test conditions, with the ten minute break after the second section, and review each one before you take another.
A passage you know nothing about.

Most of the passages you've read with me came out of a case file. The test won't be like that. You'll get a scientist on a sea creature you've never heard of, a historian on a war you skipped in school, an economist on a market in a country you've never been to, and the words will be strange on purpose. The good news is that the questions never test the subject. They test whether you can follow somebody's reasoning about it. So here's a way to read a passage when you know nothing at all.

First, read for the puzzle, not the facts. Nearly every science passage is built around something that needed explaining. An animal survives what should kill it. A lake shrinks with no drought. A medicine works in mice and fails in people. Find the puzzle in the first paragraph, and say it to yourself in a sentence. Then everything after it is one of four things: an old explanation, the evidence against it, a new explanation, or the author's judgment of where that leaves us.

Second, treat technical words as labels. If the passage says the animal enters a state called anhydrobiosis, write dry state in the margin and keep going. You don't need to know what a biologist means by it. You need to know what this passage means by it, and the passage will tell you, usually in the same sentence. A reading question is answered from the passage, never from what you happen to know.

Third, keep score on the evidence. Science passages are mostly a story about tests. Somebody predicted something, measured it, and found it or didn't. Mark each result with a plus or a minus for the explanation it bears on. Then you'll be able to answer the questions that ask what weakened the old view, or what a study showed, without rereading the whole thing.

Fourth, listen for the author's hedges. Scientists rarely sound certain, and the right attitude answer is rarely extreme. Suggests, may, appears, is consistent with: those words tell you the author is holding something at arm's length. Shows, establishes, rules out: those tell you where the author has stopped doubting. The difference between them is the answer to at least one question in most science sets. A careful author can admire a study and still doubt what it proves.

Here's a short one to practice the map. Some desert plants open their pores only at night, when the air is cool and less water escapes. They store the carbon dioxide they take in as an acid and use it in daylight with the pores shut. For years botanists thought this was purely a desert trick. Then it turned up in plants on tropical tree branches, where rain is common but water drains off the bark within hours. The author concludes that the trick answers short supply, not dry climate. Map it: the puzzle, why some plants work at night. Old view, a desert adaptation. Evidence against, the same habit where it rains. New view, an answer to water that doesn't stay. The author's stance, fairly sure, since it says answers and not may answer.

Now the questions on a passage like that. A main point question wants the author's conclusion about the puzzle: the trick answers short supply, not dry climate. A detail question asks where the night opening was found, and you point at tree branches. An inference question asks what the passage most strongly suggests the author would expect of a plant in a rainy place whose roots sit in standing water. Water stays, so the author would expect it doesn't need the trick. A function question asks why the tree branches are mentioned. They're the evidence against the old view. And an attitude question asks how the author regards the old view. Not scornful. Mistaken about the cause, and fair about the observations.

The common error on these is getting interested. You'll find a sentence about the chemistry fascinating, read it three times, and lose two minutes on a detail no question asks about. Notice it, mark it, move on. If a question needs it, you'll know exactly where it is.

How the exam asks it. Science sets ask for the main point, what a study showed, what the passage suggests that an author would expect, why a detail is mentioned, and the author's attitude toward a finding or a view. Map the puzzle, the old view, the evidence and the new view before you start the questions, and let the hedges set the strength of every answer you pick.

Speed on this test doesn't come from reading faster. It comes from not having to decide how to read. When a question type is familiar, you know what to look for before you start, and you stop rereading. So the way to get fast is to make every type boring, one at a time, and then put them back together under a clock.

Start untimed. For two weeks, take one question type a night, ten or fifteen questions of it, and do each one the slow way. Find the conclusion. Say the gap. Predict the answer in your own words. Then read the choices and sort every one: right, too strong, reversed, out of scope, true but beside the point. Write down why each wrong one is wrong. That's slow on purpose. You're building the habit that'll run by itself later.

Then time the same type in small sets. Five questions, seven minutes, the kitchen timer on the stove. Not a section. When five go cleanly, mix two types. Then all of them. You're trying to keep the slow method while the clock gets meaner, and that only works if the slow method was there to begin with.

In a full section I read the stem first. A flaw stem means go find the gap. A must be true stem means there may not be a conclusion at all, so don't hunt for one. Through the June 2027 test, a section is about twenty five questions in thirty five minutes, a little over a minute apiece, and the early ones tend to go faster. Ten in by minute ten, you're fine. Six in, and you're rereading something. I did that when I took it. I reread everything twice, like it might change.

When one's got you stuck, it's worth the same as the easy one three down. Get it to two choices, pick, flag, go. I've watched good students lose more to two questions they wrestled for four minutes than to every guess they made all morning. And half the time you come back to the flagged one and it's obvious in ten seconds.

Reading Comprehension's different. Don't read faster. Read once, with a few words in the margin for each paragraph, and then stay out of the passage unless a question sends you to a line. Through June 2027 it's four sets in thirty five minutes, call it eight and a half a set. Three on the passage, the rest on the questions, and the questions go quickly when you know where everything lives.

Keep the log I told you about. After each timed section, count the misses by type and by trap. In a month the log will show you two or three habits that cost you most of your points, and those are the ones to fix, one at a time.

How the exam asks it. Through the June 2027 test, a Logical Reasoning section is about twenty five questions in thirty five minutes, and a Reading Comprehension section is usually four sets. From August 2027 the sections get longer and the timing changes, so check lsac.org. Practice the method untimed, then in short timed sets, then in full sections, and take official PrepTests on LawHub under test timing.

Tuesday, May 11. Ana had the response printed on white paper with her pencil already all over page two, and a calculator out of a drawer that had to be older than Dani, with a solar strip that only worked if you held it under the lamp.
The phone on the desk rang before Dani had her coat off. Ana looked at the number, said Speak of her, and put it on speaker.

Ana. Meredith Sloane. Two things. When the court signs, and it will, I want your client's reference sample taken by my investigator, on our form, so nobody fights about the chain later. Fine. And? You're going to ask me why I didn't fight the test. I was going to let you tell me.

I'm not agreeing because I think you're right, Meredith said. I'm agreeing because if I'm wrong, I want to know before you do. A pause on the line. Who else is in the room? His daughter. She volunteers for me at night.

Ms. Ruiz. Her voice didn't change at all. You work for the public defender in Denver. Days. Nights I work for Ms. Brennan. Keep it exactly that way. I'd hate to have to file something about it. Then, to Ana: The jacket numbers are in there because they're true. Bring me better ones. And she was gone.
Ana hung up and looked at the phone for a while. That, she said, is the problem with fair.

People's response to the defendant's motion, filed Monday, May 3, 2027, page two. The defense makes much of the red jacket's being common. It wasn't. Mr. Galvan testified at trial that about one hundred twenty people were in the Night Owl that night. The crew list in Detective Vigil's notes, taken from the shift supervisor, has twenty one names, the defendant's among them. Even if every man on it was in the bar, fewer than one in five people in that room wore the jacket. And of all of them, exactly one man was seen fighting Travis Hensley.
Twenty one over a hundred twenty, Ana said, and punched it in under the lamp, and turned the calculator around. 17.5. Her arithmetic's fine. It usually is. So what's wrong with the argument?
A. "Seventeen and a half percent isn't rare. Nearly one person in five is a lot of any room."
B. "Then more than eighty percent didn't have one on. So the man in red was nearly sure to be one of the crew."
C. "A share isn't a count. On her own numbers, under one in five of that room is twenty one jackets. She needed one."
D. "Ronnie's hundred and twenty was a guess. He was pouring by himself all night. He never once counted a soul in there."

Say it to the judge just like that. In the margin she writes 21, and next to it 1, and a line between them. You can't identify a man with a jacket twenty one men own. She picked the number that makes twenty men sound like nobody.

That's the one. Pencil down. Flaw. The response argues from a share to a conclusion that needs a count. Twenty one men owned that jacket. Put them in a room of a hundred twenty or a room of a thousand, it's still twenty one, and a jacket only identifies somebody if he's the one man wearing it.
Ana underlined the last sentence twice. The second line came out wobbly, because Dicta picked that moment to lean her whole weight on Ana's shin. Exactly one man was seen fighting Travis Hensley.

That's the one she believes, she said. The rest of the paragraph is upholstery. She'll say it at the hearing in just those words, and she'll say it like it's arithmetic too. She set the pencil down on the page and pushed Dicta off her shin. Weaken it.

Dani knew the patrol report by heart now, the way she knew the bus schedule. Patrons' names not obtained. And Ronnie in January, across the table at the taqueria with a towel on his shoulder, saying it like it was nothing: I couldn't see over the people.
Which reply most weakens Meredith's sentence about the fight?
A. "Ronnie never saw what started it, by his own account. He only looked up when the yelling got loud."
B. "Pa told Gene that Sunday he never touched anybody. So nobody saw him fight at all."
C. "Seen by Ronnie, who couldn't see over the crowd. Nobody else in that room was ever asked."
D. "Ronnie only knew him by the jacket. Any man on the crew looked like Pa from behind a bar."

Ana says seen is a word about who was looking. Then she counts it off on the desk with the pencil: one bartender, behind the bar, a Series night, and an officer who never wrote down a single customer's name. It's true, what she wrote, she says. Because they only ever asked the one man.

Right. Now say why. Weaken. Meredith's sentence rides on the word seen. Seen by whom? By Ronnie, who couldn't see over the crowd, and he's the only one anybody ever asked. One witness asked gets you one fight seen, whatever else went on in that room.
Thursday, May 13. Meredith had attached four exhibits. Ana had read all four and put three back in the folder. The fourth she'd copied onto yellow paper, which meant pencil.

Commerce City Police Department, Property and Evidence, item record, People's Exhibit D. Item seven. Fingernail scrapings and clippings, victim T. Hensley, right and left hands. Two sealed envelopes in one evidence bag. Collected at autopsy October 28, 2007. Received October 29, 2007, at ten past eight in the morning, from Detective G. Vigil. Stored frozen, evidence room. October 30, 2007. Submitted to the state crime lab with item three, red jacket, right cuff, and item four, the victim's shirt, for DNA analysis. November 6, 2007. Lab request for item seven cancelled by Detective G. Vigil. Reason given: victim and suspect in a physical fight inside the bar before the assault; any foreign material under the victim's nails is expected from that fight and of no probative value as to who struck the victim in the lot. Items three and four to proceed. November 8, 2007. Item seven returned from the lab unopened. Seals intact. Returned to frozen storage. Audits 2012, 2017, 2022. Item present. Seals intact. April 14, 2027. Location confirmed at request of the District Attorney's Office. Seals intact. No analysis has been performed on this item.
Read it like a lease, Ana said. The easy part first. Where has it been?
A. At the state lab since 2007, where it sat untested until the jacket results came back.
B. In a freezer from the day of the autopsy on, unopened and untouched by anybody since then.
C. In the evidence room until April, when the district attorney's office had it moved for testing.
D. In the evidence freezer since 2007, to the lab and back unopened, its seals checked at every audit.

In the freezer since 2007, Dani says, to the lab and back unopened, and checked at every audit. Every audit, Ana says. Somebody opened that freezer every five years, looked at the bag, wrote seals intact and shut the door. Nobody ever lost it. Nobody ever looked inside it either.

Good. That's how you read it. Specific detail. The record puts it in frozen storage from October 29, 2007, at the lab and back unopened in November, and present with seals intact at the 2012, 2017 and 2022 audits and again in April.
Now who's talking, Ana said. Somebody in a property room typed this, a line at a time, over twenty years. Whoever typed the November entries. What does that person think about those scrapings?
A. Nothing, as far as the page shows. It writes down Gene's reason and his name, and stops there.
B. Annoyed with the lab, for sending the bag back unopened when it could have run it anyway.
C. Sure they'd never matter. It calls them of no probative value, in so many words.
D. Uneasy. It notes the seals over and over again, as if somebody knew it should have been tested.
Nothing, Ana says. Which is the right answer more often than you'd like. Whoever typed it put his name on it. They didn't put their own on his reason.
That's the one. Pencil down. Author's attitude. Neutral. The record states what was done and attributes the reason to Detective Vigil. Its author never judges whether he was right.

Now the part nobody typed, Ana said. It went to the lab in the same box as the jacket. A week later Gene cancelled it, and two days after that it came back unopened, and the jacket stayed. Why wasn't it tested? Don't tell me what you think. Tell me what this page lets you say.
A. The lab ran short of money for DNA work that fall and sent back whatever wasn't urgent.
B. Gene figured the fight explained whatever was under there, and the jacket was going ahead.
C. Phil asked the State not to test them, in case they came back with Pa's DNA under the nails.
D. Gene thought the scrapings would only show Travis's own skin, so there'd be nothing to look at.
Expected, Ana says. He doesn't say I had my guy. He says expected. That's how you say I had my guy in a property room.

Right. Now say why. Inference. The reason given is that anything under the nails would be expected from the fight, and the same entry sends the jacket and shirt ahead. So the record supports that he thought the test couldn't tell him anything new, with the jacket already on its way.

Ana read Gene's line out loud, the way she read things she meant to take apart. Any foreign material under the victim's nails is expected from that fight and of no probative value as to who struck the victim in the lot.
Dani didn't hear the end of it. She was still on expected.
He's right about part of it, she said. Ana looked up. His will be under there. I saw his neck that Sunday.

Then she told it, the way it had come back to her in January at the bathroom sink. Noon on a Sunday, the bathroom door open, her father shaving, who never shaved on Sundays. A square of tissue under his jaw on the left side with a red dot coming through it. Cut myself, mija. Go back to sleep. A nick under his collar by the time Gene came at three. She said it to the edge of the desk. She'd never once said it out loud, and it came out shorter than it had been in her head for four months. The last time she'd told anybody what she saw in that house on that Sunday, she was fifteen, and there were twelve of them listening, and she'd been sure.

Ana didn't write anything down. She laid the pencil crosswise on the yellow page and kept her hand on it. Since January, she said. Not a question. I didn't know what it was. It's what Ronnie said it was. Two men with their hands on each other in a bar. She picked the pencil back up. Good. Now it's mine too. I'd a lot rather have it from you than from a lab.
She tapped Gene's line. So say his is there. What's wrong with this sentence?
A. Gene cancelled the test before the jacket ever came back from the state lab, so he couldn't have known anything yet about whose blood was on that cuff.
B. Pa told Gene that Sunday he never fought anybody that night, so Gene had no reason in the world to expect his skin under there, from the bar or anywhere else.
C. It assumes the fight inside is the only way anybody's skin got under there. Tests can often tell two men apart, and the man at the curb got close enough to hit him.
D. The tests are a lot better now than they were back in 2007. A lab today could find things under those nails that Gene never once pictured, sitting in his kitchen.

Ana writes TWO MEN on the yellow page and boxes it. Expected tells you what'll be there, she says. It doesn't tell you what else will. If there's one and it's his, Meredith wrote the right brief. If there's two. She doesn't finish it. Dani doesn't ask her to.

Good. That's how you read it. Strengthen or weaken a passage claim. Gene's line says the nails can't tell you anything about the lot, since Luis's DNA ought to be there from the bar. That holds only if he's the only man whose DNA could be there. If a test can separate two men, and the man at the curb got close enough to strike Travis, a second profile would be about the lot.

Saturday, May 15, nine in the morning, Gene's notebook out of its freezer bag on Ana's desk. Ana had flagged page eleven with a strip of yellow paper. A column of names in Gene's square hand, two of them misspelled and fixed, and across the top, in capitals, the Platte Valley day shift for October 27, per the supervisor. Twenty one names. The fourth one down was RUIZ, L.
She took her own phone out to the landing, shut Ana's door behind her, and called Northglenn.

It's Gene. He was out on the drive with the hose; she could hear it running. She asked about page eleven. Off the phone with the supervisor, he said. Sunday night, at the kitchen table. My wife was doing the crossword. A pause. I remember thinking, that's a lot of red.
Then she read him the November line off the yellow copy, word for word. The hose shut off. He let it sit. She could hear a sprinkler going two yards down from him.

That's me, he said. That line's mine. I called the lab and pulled it. Another pause. I'll tell you why, and you won't like it. I got called to that bar ten, eleven times over the years, patrol and after. Every time one went out to the lot, it was the same two who'd started it inside. Every single time. So I figured the nails would tell me what I already knew, and the lab had a line out the door.
Gene's reasoning from the ten or eleven calls is most vulnerable to which criticism?
A. "Eleven fights isn't very many to build a rule on, Gene. That's not even one a year."
B. "You pulled it because you knew what it would show. You didn't want to find another man."
C. "Then you should've tested it anyway, Gene. If you were right, it would only have proved it."
D. "Those were fights somebody called in, Gene. The ones nobody called in never got to you."

Nothing on the line. Then a sound like a laugh with no fun in it. Nobody calls about the ones that go fine, he says. Or the ones that go out back where nobody's looking. He's quiet again. Eleven I got called to. That's all I ever knew about that bar.

That's the one. Pencil down. Flaw. Gene builds a rule from the fights he was called to, and those aren't a fair sample of the bar's fights. A fight that went out back and ended where nobody saw it never became a call, so the rule was built from exactly the cases most likely to fit it.

Sunday, May 16, she built the count at the kitchen table on her laptop, with page eleven copied out beside it and the 2007 box score open in another window. Game 3. A Saturday night at Coors Field, the Rockies' first World Series game at home, and Boston fans all over the city in red.

Dani's draft: red, the night of Saturday, October 27, 2007. Under it, her caption: The city was full of red that night. Fifty thousand at the game alone, Boston everywhere. The jacket was the most common thing in Denver, so it couldn't point at anybody.

Four bars. At Coors Field for Game 3, forty nine thousand and change. On Gene's crew list, twenty one. Crew besides Pa that anybody interviewed, none. Men seen fighting Travis, one. The first bar ran clear across the screen, and the other three were slivers. She had her thumb on send a long while, and then she didn't send it. She read the caption the way Ana would, with a pencil she didn't have.
What, if anything, is wrong with the caption's reasoning?
A. The city's red doesn't count. Almost none of those fifty thousand were near that lot at 11:15.
B. Nothing. If red was everywhere in Denver that night, then it was everywhere in that lot too.
C. Fans in red jerseys aren't men in red jackets. Consuelo said jacket, not shirt, every time.
D. It's right, but too small. It should count the whole metro area, every fan who watched in a bar.

She deletes the first bar. Without it the chart looks foolish: twenty one, nothing, one. Three stubs. That's the chart. She sends Ana that one, with no caption at all, and Ana writes back a few minutes later. Better.

Right. Now say why. Flaw. The caption measures red across a whole city and draws a conclusion about one parking lot. The people to count are the ones who could have been at that curb at a quarter past eleven. Most of the city's red was miles away, so the city's number can't show the jacket meant nothing there.

Tuesday, May 18. She'd spent Sunday night on page eleven, and two lunch hours in her car with her own phone. A legal pad with twenty one lines and what she'd found beside each one. Four obituaries. One man in Texas. A union newsletter from 2011 with three of the names in a softball photo. Phone numbers for six.
If I call all twenty, she said, somebody remembers who went out back. Somebody saw something. We find the man at the curb.
Ana looked at the legal pad a long time, both hands flat on the desk on either side of it.
We don't have to prove who, she said. We have to prove it wasn't him.

At the trial the State had to show it was him, and in 2008 that had been Phil's whole closing. That was before a verdict. After one, the weight sits on your side of the table, and Ana had been saying so since March in one way or another.
So tell me what your count shows, Ana said. And what it doesn't.
A. "It shows the jacket can't pick him out of twenty one. It doesn't put any of the others at that curb."
B. "It shows twenty other men could just as easily have been the man at the curb that night."
C. "It shows one of the crew most likely did it. So we start calling and we find out which one."
D. "It shows Pa almost certainly wasn't the man at the curb. One in twenty one is under five percent."

That's the size of it, Ana says. Probably wasn't him, on the evidence, is what we owe the court. Who is somebody else's job. Maybe nobody's, ever. She tears the legal pad page off and puts it in the folder. Not the trash. The folder.

Good. That's how you read it. Most strongly supported. Twenty one men had that jacket, so the jacket alone can't identify Luis. That's all the count supports. It doesn't put another crew member in the lot, and it doesn't settle where Luis was.

If you call anybody, Ana said, you call to ask one thing, and you ask it nicely. Meredith says the jacket wasn't common. We say it was common enough that it couldn't point at one man in that lot. What fact, if we could get it, does the most for us?
Downstairs a washer hit its spin cycle and the whole floor hummed with it. Dicta opened one eye and shut it.
A. That every man on the crew list was issued the very same red jacket by the refinery that year.
B. That a dozen of the crew were still in the bar in their jackets after Ronnie threw Pa out.
C. That Boston fans had bought red jackets all over Denver that weekend, at the game and after.
D. That Pa had worn that same jacket into the Night Owl every Saturday for years before that one.

After Ronnie threw him out, Ana says. After. That's the word. She writes it on a card, STILL THERE AFTER 10:45?, and puts it on top of page eleven. Ask that. Don't ask them who. Nobody's going to tell a stranger on the phone who, and anyway it isn't our question.

That's the one. Pencil down. Strengthen. The claim is that the jacket couldn't single Luis out in the lot. The jackets that matter are the ones still around after he left, because those are the men who could have been out there at a quarter past eleven. A count of them supports the claim most directly.
Tuesday night a Denver news site ran it. Celia didn't send it this time. Dani found it herself at eleven, in bed, which was the wrong place.

News item, Tuesday, May 18, 2027. Prosecutors in Adams County won't oppose DNA testing in the case of a man convicted of a 2007 death outside a Commerce City bar, according to a court filing. Luis Ruiz, 62, is serving forty years for second degree murder in the death of Travis Hensley, 31. His lawyer says evidence collected in 2007 was never tested, and that the red work jacket at the center of the trial was common among men in the bar that night. Shannon Hensley, the victim's sister, said she wasn't surprised. "Let them count jackets," she said. "Say there were twenty. One of them fought my brother and went out the back after him."
On the nightstand, in her own capitals from Sunday, before Ana: SAY 20 JACKETS IN THE BAR. PA IS ONE. 19 IN 20 IT WASN'T HIM.
She read Shannon's sentence four times. Then her own card. Then the sentence again.
What should Dani make of what Shannon said?
A. She's wrong, and somebody ought to tell her. Write Shannon tonight and walk her through the twenty.
B. The twenty weren't alike. Only one of them had just fought Travis and been thrown out the back.
C. Lots of the Boston fans wore red jerseys too. Twenty jackets leaves out every red shirt in the room.
D. Nobody knows how many of the crew were really in the bar. Twenty is a guess, and maybe a high one.

She doesn't write to Shannon. She writes Shannon's sentence on the card under her own, in Shannon's words, because it's the better argument and somebody's going to have to answer it. Then she turns the light off and lies there a while, thinking about a woman who'd had to say that to a reporter on the phone.

Right. Now say why. Weaken. A base rate treats every man in a group as equally likely. The twenty jackets weren't equal: one belonged to the man who had just fought Travis and gone out the back. A fact that sets one member apart cuts the base rate's force.
Wednesday, May 19, seven. Her step. The recording, and then him, before she could say anything at all. Queen goes home.

She'd carried the board down to the step for once, and she moved it there on her knees. His queen off the long file, back to the square it started the game on, and the file in front of her king was just a file again, closed, with nobody at the far end of it. Four weeks he'd looked at it. That was what he'd been looking at.
You saw it, he said. At the table. I watched you see it.

He wanted the news, so she gave it to him. Meredith wasn't fighting the test. Ana said the judge could sign any day, and then the lab would get the scrapings, and nobody could say how long after that. And then they know, he said. Whatever it is.
He didn't ask her what she hoped it was. He never asked her that.
Ana's card was on the step beside her, the State's timeline in pencil.
Ana's timeline card. 10:45, OUT THE BACK. 11:04, STILL OUT HERE. 11:15, MAN IN RED AT THE CURB, RAN NORTH ON FOOT. 11:21, POLICE.

Thirty minutes from the back door to the curb, and the State needed him in that lot the whole time, or gone and back. She had him on the line, and maybe one question before the recording told them a minute was left.
Which question would best test the State's timeline?
A. "Pa, what did Travis say to you inside, right before you hit him? What was it?"
B. "Pa, why'd you go to the Night Owl that night at all, with Ma working and nobody home?"
C. "Pa, did anybody see you leave the Night Owl that night? Anybody at all, out in the lot?"
D. "Pa, after Ronnie threw you out, was your truck still in that lot at a quarter past eleven?"

It's quiet a long time. Somebody on his end is yelling about the microwave. I drove home, mija, he says. I told you. I told everybody. It's an answer. It isn't to the question she asked, which was about a quarter past eleven. She lets it sit there on the line between them and doesn't take it back.

Good. That's how you read it. Evaluate the argument. The State needs him in that lot from 10:45 to 11:15, or gone and back. Say the truck was still there at 11:15: he never left, which fits the State's timeline, though it has to explain why he ran off on foot. Say it was gone: he'd driven away, and the State has to explain how he got back to the curb without it. One answer helps the timeline and the other hurts it, and that's the test.
Thursday, May 20, at ten after two, her phone buzzed on her desk at the office with Ana's name on it, and she took it out to the stairwell, the way she took every call that wasn't the office's.
Signed, Ana said. I'm sending you the page. Read it on the stairs.

District Court, Adams County. Order on the defendant's motion for postconviction DNA testing, Thursday, May 20, 2027. On the People's written stipulation, the Court finds that the requirements for testing are met. The fingernail scrapings collected from Travis Hensley on October 28, 2007, Commerce City Police Department Item 7, shall be released to the Colorado Bureau of Investigation for DNA testing. The parties shall confer on the methods of testing. The defendant shall provide a reference sample. The Court reserves ruling on the remaining claims until the results are filed. Martin Esquibel, District Court Judge.

When? When they get to it. They have a line, and now we're in it. A bus sighed at the stop on Federal behind her. And whatever's under there goes into the state's databases and the national one. That's the law too. It runs both directions. Then: Go back to work. Write your father tonight. He'll want it on paper.

She wrote him at the kitchen table after supper, one page, the judge's sentence copied out word for word, because he'd read it six times and he'd want the words. Then she couldn't study. She sat with the prep book open to a page she'd already done and did the only thing she'd been any good at all month. She counted.

Twenty one names on page eleven. A hundred twenty people in the room, if Ronnie was right. Eleven fights Gene got called to. Forty nine thousand nine hundred eighty three at Coors Field. One man seen fighting, by the one man anybody asked. Everybody in that bar had finally been counted by somebody, years late. Everybody but one.
A beer and a Sprite, every time he came up. Later on, just the Sprite.
Ronnie never counted the Sprite. Nobody had. A Sprite isn't anybody. It's a glass going back to a table by the hallway, where a big man in a wet shirt was bent over some, yelling down at something.

Teo drank Sprite. At ten he'd have had it with every meal if anybody let him. Their mother bought it in twelve packs and hid one in the dryer so he couldn't finish it in a weekend, and he always found it, and she always acted surprised.

Ten years old, Pa had said at Sterling, about the pawn. Some kid. Nobody. A boy crying Papi in the lot at ten to eleven. Teo had called him Papi until he was eleven or so, when he was hurt or scared, and Pa the rest of the time. She'd never forgotten it. In Consuelo's kitchen in February she'd thought of him for one second, and put the thought back where it came from, and kept it there.
The envelope was in the book, marking her page. She took it out and turned it over. WHO WAS THE KID? in her capitals from the Sterling lot. Under it she wrote his name. Not in capitals.
There were six numbers from page eleven in her phone, and she hadn't called one of them. She didn't call them now.
She looked at his name. Then at her phone. He hadn't answered the last one, the pawn, in almost five weeks.

Three weeks from Saturday she'd sit in a test center for most of a morning with her phone in a locker. Seats opened next Tuesday, and she'd ask for Saturday the twelfth, the one morning nobody had to take off work for. She could drive herself. She'd driven herself to Sterling in the dark.
She typed it the way their mother had typed every text she ever sent, a capital at the front and a period at the end, like a letter.
A text from Dani. Can you drive me on the 12th.
She put the phone face down on the table and got as far as standing up. It buzzed before she'd pushed her chair in. Four seconds, maybe.

She sat back down. Downstairs the new washer had finished its load an hour ago, and she left it there. She turned the phone over so she could see that word. Then she opened the book to a page she hadn't done yet. Page 212. A dog groomer in Fort Collins, a coupon, a bad inference about Tuesdays. She got it wrong. She did it again.
